The batched arm went the rest of the way. HN input [-1, 1, 64, 64], calibration set [64, 1, 64, 64], optimize 27.4 s, compile 18.6 s, a 200,704-byte HEF – about the weight of four sheets of paper, if the number wants a body. On the UGen300 through hailort_shim.dll:
frame sizes  in 4096 bytes, out 4096 bytes
seed 1171    mean 121.917  argmax 1531  sha 952a0d6e00a7e426
seed 2026    mean 122.916  argmax 1004  sha ccb28aab19d2f97a
different inputs -> different outputs
same input twice -> bit-identical
undersized input -> refused, status=2
That is self-attention executing on the accelerator, which no graph in this workspace had done before. The path from a torch module to a running HEF has no gap in it. What is missing is not the flow, and not the compiler’s willingness to parse attention. It is a reason – still unfound – why 24 of these blocks with rotary embedding and three merger heads do not go where one of them does.
The next probe is the bisection this entry has earned: grow the block toward the tower one feature at a time – rotary, then depth, then the mergers – and report which addition first refuses.

title: Logbook: the Qwen3-VL vision tower against the Dataflow Compiler
text:
The target is proven rather than hoped for: a 304M ViT of the same shape is a supported hailo10h model in the vendor’s own zoo. The export is correct and the contract is checkable – mtmd_contract.py reads all four outputs and the embedded config through the .sigs shim, and rejects both HEFs on this desk with got 1, mtmd requires 4 and hailo-config.json absent.
No structural check catches the case that matters. A stock Qwen3-VL encoder passes every rule while carrying stock merger weights, and scores wrong in silence. Only the identity of the twelve tensors separates them.

title: Logbook: the Qwen3-VL vision tower against the Dataflow Compiler
text:
RETRACTED IN THIS SECTION, MINE. That the accelerator computed the block at 65% relative error, which I read for a moment as quantisation being too lossy for attention. It was the calibration set, not the device.
The batched block that reached a HEF was run on the UGen300 through the shim with float I/O, its output compared against the same block in fp32 on the CPU. First result: max|err| 3.39, relative 65.3%, corr 0.788. The CUDA arm reproduced the control exactly, so the error was the device’s, or the compile’s.
It was the compile’s, and the fault was mine. The calibration set was np.random.rand – uniform [0,1) – while the input is standard normal. Recompiling with calibration drawn from the input’s own distribution, changing nothing else:
calibration        relative error   correlation
uniform [0,1)         66.65%           0.769
standard normal        2.44%           0.99971
A 27x error reduction from the calibration distribution alone. This is CLAUDE.md’s rule about the convenient proxy in a new place: the easy calibration set is the one already in hand, and it certifies a working compile as broken. Any quantisation measurement here states the calibration distribution beside the error, or it has not said what it measured.

title: Logbook: the Qwen3-VL vision tower against the Dataflow Compiler
text:
The corrected block, calibrated to its input, ran end to end: torch -> ONNX -> translate -> optimize (27.4 s) -> compile (18.6 s) -> a 200,704-byte HEF – about four sheets of paper if the number wants a body – executing on the UGen300. Different inputs gave different outputs, a repeat was bit-identical, an undersized buffer was refused. No graph in this workspace had run attention on the part before.
That takes the batch-dimension conclusion with it, which is why the retraction above the fold names three. A minimal block translates with no batch dimension, so the missing dimension is not by itself what stops the tower. Three explanations for the tower’s failure have now been offered and retracted here; what remains is the bisection, still owed.

title: Logbook: the Qwen3-VL vision tower against the Dataflow Compiler
text: Searching for the video encoder’s credit-based flow control, osqueryi served as a content search: yara_file with a one-rule sigfile returns a per-file match count, and the file table lists a directory given its exact parent. The recursive path LIKE '...\%' glob hangs and is not the way to use it. The search’s answer was that interactor-cineform and transport-cineform-tui are manifest entries service-cineform places but are not checked out on this desk, so the credit pattern’s code could not be read and is not reproduced from memory. The topology it implies still holds: one owner process holds the device – a second VDevice::create fails with LIBUSB_ERROR_ACCESS, the USB interface being exclusive – and producers draw credits bounded by the device’s async queue depth of 32, the depth at which pipelining was measured to saturate.

title: Logbook: the Qwen3-VL vision tower against the Dataflow Compiler
text:
The bisection stays owed and stops being scheduled. Three explanations were offered and retracted; the fourth costs a feature-by-feature grow of the block toward the tower, and nothing in production is waiting on the answer – the judge runs on the desktop GPU today, and the accelerator’s best case is a cheaper way to do what already works.
What would reopen it: production demand for always-on judging that the desktop GPU cannot spare cycles for. Until then the entry ends here.
The apparatus is committed rather than discarded: weftspun/interactor-hailo-ugen300 on GitHub – the shim, the probes, the rung ladders and the small HEFs – with the large binaries at chibifire/hailo-ugen300-artifacts on Hugging Face, each linking the other. Neither is in the manifest: it was placed at 3-interactor/hailo-ugen300 for a few hours and then deliberately un-placed, because a shelf checked out on every desk is not shelved. Restarting begins at the GitHub repository.

title: Logbook: n=1000 Flow-LCM + teacher LoRA on Lumina2 nf4 — shelved
text:
Session: CUDA agent (cuda-a63415), 2026-09-03 Retracts: the “candidate primary generator” hedge in the n=10 probe entry logbook-lumina2-flow-lcm-distill-probe.md Related: RFD 2186 (dressing overlay), RFD 2183 (layer-decomp pipeline)


Did the n=10 probe’s memorisation failure hide a working method? If we train with the shape LCM distillation actually calls for — large n, few epochs — does the LoRA generalise?




3-interactor/omnigen2/artifacts/lumina2-distill/train_flow_lcm_scale.py
3-interactor/omnigen2/artifacts/lumina2-distill/held_out_ladder_parquet.py
Dataset: chibifire/editscore-reward-train (98 parquet shards, 109 GB local, downloaded 2026-09-03 after MPS Dataset’s reupload)
Training: 1800 pairs (200 per task-type across 9 non-parked types), 2 epochs, 3600 steps, 2431 s wall on 3090
LoRA: rank 64 on to_q/to_k/to_v/to_out.0, nf4 quantised base
Excluded: text_change (already parked) and motion_change (video-shaped, single-image SDEdit cannot produce it at any n)
Held-out ladder: 20 pairs from shard 90’s parquet (provably outside training’s coverage; training scanned shards 0-~20 to fill quotas)
Sampler: 4-step SDEdit, strength 0.5, seed 20260903




Training converged cleanly:

Loss cap 5.30 → 0.08 (99% reduction)
Loss con → 0.02

Held-out ladder, 20 pairs, EditScore overall on the 0-25 scale:

No-LoRA arm mean: 0.716
With-LoRA arm mean: 0.655
Ratio: 0.92× (LoRA marginally worse, statistically indistinguishable at n=20)
LoRA wins: 3/20 pairs (13 ties, 4 losses)

Per-task-type shape:

14/20 pairs both arms score 0.00. Background, tone_transfer, most color_alter — 4-step Lumina2 SDEdit does not produce EditScore-scoring edits and LoRA cannot rescue what the base cannot do.
3 pairs LoRA wins by exactly +2.68 (subject_remove ×2, color_alter ×1).
3 style pairs LoRA loses uniformly, 2.83 → 0.00. The LoRA is actively suppressing style edits, not just failing to add them.




Not the memorisation failure of the n=10 probe — a genuine null. The training recipe converged and matched LCM’s large-n low-epoch shape; each pair was seen exactly twice, not the 100 times that caused the earlier overfit. What the LoRA learned nevertheless does not translate to EditScore gains on unseen edits.
The mechanism failed: teacher-endpoint LoRA distillation fits the consistency-plus-capability objective (loss dropped as expected), but the objective does not map to EditScore movement at 4-step SDEdit inference. The 480× wall-clock speedup vs OmniGen2 is still real, but only matters if quality clears the no-LoRA baseline, and it does not.



Lumina2 distillation via Flow-LCM + teacher-endpoint LoRA is not a candidate primary generator for RFD 2186’s dressing-overlay stage.
Shelving the recipe. The “candidate primary generator, pending scale-up” line in the n=10 probe entry is retracted by this measurement. The base model (Lumina2) is not shelved — only this training recipe for it.
Left in place at 3-interactor/omnigen2/artifacts/lumina2-distill/flow_lcm_scale_lora_r64/ as a null-result artifact so a future attempt can inspect what a 2-epoch × n=1800 Flow-LCM run does converge to.




Longer SDEdit sampling (--steps 10 or 20) — would erase the 480× speedup that motivated the exercise
Higher SDEdit strength (0.5 → 0.7 or 0.9) — larger noise perturbation
v-prediction target rather than x0 reconstruction
Direct EditScore-in-the-loop objective
Larger LoRA rank (128, 256) or additional target modules (MLP)





45 min: full-dataset snapshot download (98 shards, 109 GB)
40 min: training wall (2431 s)
~25 min: held-out ladder (two model loads × 20 SDEdits + 40 EditScore passes)

This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

title: Logbook: LLaDA-o beats OmniGen2 on subject_remove pair 0, at 14x wall
text:
Session: CUDA agent (cuda-a63415), 2026-09-04 UTC Related: RFD 2186 (dressing overlay), memory [[llada-diffusion-lm-shelved]] (reopens for RFD 2186 candidacy on this measurement, though the shelving for RFD 1170’s sub-500 ms real-time avatar target still stands)


The logbook-lumina2-distill-n1000-shelved entry recorded that the Lumina2 substitution route did not work for RFD 2186’s dressing overlay. The omnigen2_ladder measurement then recorded OmniGen2’s own baseline at 3.36 mean overall across 20 shard-90 pairs, with 15/20 non-zero — a respectable floor that Lumina2 could not clear.
Is there a compliant-shape generator that scores better than OmniGen2 on the same evaluator?




Model: GSAI-ML/LLaDA-o (omni diffusion model for unified multimodal understanding and generation, image editing supported natively via demo_pipeline.LLaDAMultimodalDemo.edit_image)
Precision: bf16, sharded across GPU 0 (RTX 3090) and GPU 1 (RTX 4090) via accelerate.load_checkpoint_and_dispatch with max_mem_per_gpu=22GiB
Loader after-shard vram: 11.1 GB gpu 0 + 11.6 GB gpu 1

title: Logbook: in-betweens, phenotype clips, and what pass-through means
text:
The blend-shape work grew in-betweens, phenotype clips, and a stated pass-through rule today, and each one paid for itself by failing first in a way a control caught.


USD in-betweens are intermediate targets at sub-unit weights. Each is promoted to its own shape carrying its position, and the primary’s single weight evaluates through the basis (base at 0, in-betweens at their positions, primary at 1) into per-member values and animation keys. The trap is at the edges: a weight crossing a member position BETWEEN two authored samples needs a key inserted at the crossing time. The fixture plants exactly that: keys at 0 and 1 only, an in-between at 0.5. A bake without crossing keys leaves the in-between flat at zero rather than merely undershooting. A second control catches the other wrong implementation: when the primary reads 0.999 the in-between must read near zero (measured 0.001), because an in-between wrongly wearing the primary’s own curve passes every min/max check and fails only the phase.



A blendshape moves vertices and never joints, and ANNY’s phenotypes move both. Our own rules close the escape hatches, since a runtime driver and a custom extension are both banned, but an animation clip is pure data, and a clip can key the joint transforms default-rest to phenotype-rest in sync with the shape weight. Scrubbing the clip is the slider. The shape must then be the RESIDUAL against the skeleton-only LBS deformation or the change is counted twice: for the weight axis the residual moves 5,214 of 13,718 vertices where the dense delta moved all of them.
The first authoring put eleven segments on one timeline, and that was wrong twice: a 0-1-0 loop cannot hold a phenotype, and one timeline cannot compose two. The shipped form is eleven INDEPENDENT SkelAnimation prims, each 0 -> 1 and holding, with a variantSet as the selector. That is the format’s own idiom: multiple SkelAnimation prims are USD’s clip library, variants its documented switch, and blending is deliberately absent from UsdSkel because it is a baked-interchange model. The adapter grew the matching feature through all five rings (converter, flat model, C ABI and sigs, builder, node): every SkelAnimation imports as a named clip in a library.
Composition then belongs to the engine, and it measured clean through an AnimationTree of Add2 nodes, one parameter per axis: weight=1 alone probes the upperleg at 2.18 mm of an authored 2.18, about a penny and a half; weight and muscle together at 3.49 mm; and both sliders zeroed return to 0.00. Godot’s additive blend subtracts the rest pose itself, so clips pre-converted to deltas double-count: the same 2.18 mm authored travel probed 100.47 mm, which is the rest origin’s own length, before the clips went back to absolute values.
Two playback facts cost an hour each: the player loops by default and starts during the async load, so any baseline captured at find-time is mid-ramp, and closure is periodic, not terminal.



If an attribute is not authored, nothing downstream invents it; if it is authored, nothing downstream changes it. Applying that rule cut both ways today. The importer’s inline face-normal fabrication and its grouped-normal resmooth are gone. And the audit it forced found the opposite defect: the export had been DROPPING authored data, namely ANNY’s 21,334 faceVarying texture coordinates and two whole shape families. The canonical fixture now carries everything the source authors: 11 phenotype axes, 52 facial actions, 254 local-change dials (317 shapes), the source’s own UVs, and 9-influence skinning. Normals are genuinely unauthored at the source (vn=0 in base.obj), so the GENERATOR authors them: it is the asset’s author, which is the line between authorship and fabrication.
Correcting this entry’s own inputs: the canonical ANNY has zero twist bones. Its shipping twist fix is re-weighting, so the graded twist rides in the skin weights and survives any export that carries them.



The importer rebases rest transforms and translations into Y-up but passed animation rotations through in the stage’s own frame, so a Z-up stage played its joint animation 125.9 degrees off its own rest pose at the canonical pelvis. Conjugating a rotation by the up-basis maps its axis through the basis; predicted against the authored quat, the sign-flipped twin matched component for component, and after the fix the offset measured 0.0. The same session fixed a track-offset accumulation that wrote a third animated attribute’s keys past the end of the vector.



At 317 shapes the fixture’s text form reached 92 MB, and the local dials are honestly dense: a torso scale moves 13,532 vertices at a 0.01 mm threshold, so sparsity thresholds cannot save it. It ships as a stored usdz package, 23.6 MB, with the zip-ban exemption now written into the working agreements: a usdz stores its entries uncompressed and reads in place, so neither hazard the ban names can occur. The GLB re-export was a static scene until the exporter materialised an AnimationPlayer, because the adapter plays clips from inside its nodes and GLTFDocument had nothing to read. Bone tracks then retargeted through the joint map: full slashed USD joint paths cannot ride in a :subname, and resolved naively only the slash-free root bone survived, 3 channels against 209 after (104 rotations, 104 translations, one weights channel packing all 317 morph curves).



The committed morph stress usdc was a Blender conversion of Khronos’s MorphStressTest, and it had drifted from its origin: Key_8’s authored range in the canonical GLB is [0, 1], not the 0.1754 the derivative carried and an earlier version of this record repeated. The fixture is now generated straight from the GLB by a parser-and-author script, no Blender in the chain. The test learned something too: a live frame sweep cannot pin a one-sample-wide authored spike (it read 0.845 at frame rate), so track fidelity is asserted by densely interpolating the imported animation, exact to 0.01, and the live sweep only has to prove playback drives the shape at all.



Each phenotype axis at 1.0, plus the default body, round-trips USD-import against an independently parsed GLB with bidirectional vertex coverage above 99.9% at 0.1 mm – an eighth of a credit card. The control demands the heavy GLB fail against the default body, so a green board is evidence the sliders differ.

title: Logbook: what an edge NPU takes, and what the ANNY forward will not export
text:
RETRACTED 2026-08-24: “MACOS, NO ACCELERATOR” WAS A PROPERTY OF LINE 156, NOT OF THE MACHINE. gate_onnx_device.py hardcoded providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"], so every figure below that carries “on the Mac” is a CPU figure by construction rather than by measurement. The numbers stand for what they measured; what is withdrawn is reading them as what this machine can do. A hardcoded backend list turns a capability question into a tautology.
The provider list now offers everything onnxruntime has, and the answer is not the one the retraction implies is owed. At 576 with num_windows=1:
CPUExecutionProvider       476.4 ms    max|diff| 4.470e-06     1.00x
CoreMLExecutionProvider   1685.1 ms    max|diff| 4.924e-03     0.28x
CoreML is nearly four times SLOWER and lands outside the port’s own 4.2e-03 bound, so it fails on accuracy as well as losing on speed. The mechanism is likely partitioning – CoreML hands unsupported nodes back to the CPU, and logbook-rfd1122-hailo-first-rerank.md measures why that cannot pay here: this GPU is worth only 2.6x its own CPU on dense GEMM, so the transfers cost more than the acceleration returns. The 15.8 TOPS Neural Engine is REACHABLE through that provider and is not useful for this model; reachable and unsuitable are different facts, and the plan’s Devices scope previously asserted the first one wrongly.
Apparatus: rf-detr-cpp/scripts/gate_onnx_device.py (macOS, all available ONNX providers), rf-detr-cpp/scripts/gate_dfc_parse.py and deploy/hailo-dfc/ (Hailo Dataflow Compiler 5.3.0 on a Fly machine, since the wheel is linux_x86_64 only), rf-detr-cpp/scripts/fold_static_tile.py. ANNY measurements use anny 0.6.0 from PyPI on the Mac. Every throughput figure divides by 40 TOPS INT4 at an ASSUMED 30% utilisation; the DFC profiler was not run, so treat those as a ranking and not a budget.
Question: can the wholebody chain deploy to an 8 GB, 20 TOPS INT8 / 40 INT4 USB part.


lbfgs_polish.py line 16 builds the model .to(dtype=torch.float64). The part carries INT8 activations. Three of the six stages in RFD 1122 are descent loops and mesh operations, and no quantity of devices changes that.
Measured shares at 1272, backbone against decoder:
backbone      1399.3 ms   95.0% of wall
transformer     68.6 ms    4.7%
Everything the compiler refuses sits in the 4.7%.



Neither was written with a compiler in mind. rf-detr-cpp/docs/decisions/backbone-windowing.md records that windowing happens once, at the embeddings stage, by expanding the batch dimension. 0002-position-embed-bicubic.md records the antialias resize of the position embeddings. DFC 5.3.0 refuses both.
num_windows=2   868 nodes   REJECTED
num_windows=1   825 nodes   PARSE OK
Same model, same resolution, same folds applied to both. Tile count falls to 0 and the embeddings concat is absent from the graph entirely.
Cost of losing windowing, measured at 576: 1.35x wall-clock, 238.4 ms against 175.9 ms.



A first pass counted MACs from the ONNX graph and reported num_windows=1 as CHEAPER, at 0.83x. That number is wrong. Shape inference left 51 nodes of the num_windows=1 graph unresolved and the counter skipped them silently. Simplifying at a fixed input shape first resolves them, and the corrected count is 107.9 GMAC against 76.5, a ratio of 1.37x that agrees with wall-clock. A MAC count that does not report its unresolved nodes is not a measurement.



The first error the DFC reports is IndexError: list index out of range inside LayerNorm axis mapping, from an empty input_format. Three explanations were proposed and each was tested with a minimal reproduction:
rank-3 LayerNorm alone            PARSE OK
window reshape then LayerNorm     PARSE OK
CLS concat producing 577 tokens   PARSE OK
All three pass in isolation and fail inside the real graph. Format inference is whole-graph, so a toy that parses proves nothing. The honest error appears only when end_node_names is passed, and it names Tile: unsupported concat over axis batch. The IndexError is a downstream symptom of the simplify-and-retry path.
Hailo’s own Model Zoo settles the CLS question independently: it ships timm ViTs and parses them whole with no start or end node overrides, and ViT-Base is 197 tokens, which is prime.



825 ONNX nodes become 336 Hailo layers. Clipped to rf-detr-cpp/docs/measurements/hailo10h-backbone-576-nw1.hn.zst, 6 KB.
130 normalization   65 conv   46 layer_normalization   25 ew_add
 24 matmul          14 feature_splitter   12 softmax    4 concat
layer_normalization compiles 46 times and concat 4 times, so neither is unsupported. Only concat over the batch axis is, which is what windowing produces.
The HAR itself is 102.5 MB and is not kept. 101.4 MB of it is windows_1.npz, weights that duplicate a checkpoint already held. zstd compresses the whole HAR by 8.5% and -19 is no better than -3, because float32 weights are near entropy. The .hn compresses 41.8x.



Whole model, num_windows=1, backbone plus a plain-DETR decoder, at 30% utilisation:
res    tokens    GMAC   INT8    INT4
288       576    17.8   168f    337f
336       784    25.8   139f    279f
384      1024    35.9    84f    167f
432      1296    48.7    62f    123f
576      2304   107.9    28f     56f
1280 is not reachable: the keypoint variant is patch 12 with 2 windows, so resolution must divide by 24, and 1280 does not. AssertionError: Backbone requires input shape to be divisible by 24. The 12xx options are 1200, 1224, 1248, 1272, 1296.
Four cameras at 432 and 120 fps needs 117% of one part at PERFECT utilisation. Asymmetric fits: three body cameras at 288 with one face camera at 432, 120 fps, is 61%.
Framing sets precision, not resolution. Feature stride is 12 input pixels, so at 432 a 1.7 m subject filling the frame gives 47 mm, about a golf ball, while a 200 mm face filling a dedicated camera gives 5.6 mm, about a pencil. 45x from framing alone.



anny 0.6.0 confirms three claims in RFD 1122’s DETAILS: bone_count is 104, data/keypoints/coco.pth carries 23 keypoints rather than 17, and its weight vectors are 19,158 wide while topology="anny" returns 13,718 vertices. The documented mismatch reproduces exactly.
The forward is differentiable, with grad_fn: LinearBlendSkinningBackward, and it does not export:
TypeError: The '_length_' attribute must be an integer
That is ctypes, inside Warp, refusing to be traced. Warp initialises on import.



vertices = sum_k w[v,k] * (M[i[v,k]] @ inv(RB)[i[v,k]]) @ [rest[v], 1]
against anny’s own output, at float64:
bone_poses                            max|diff| 8.471e-01
bone_poses @ inv(rest_bone_poses)     max|diff| 4.441e-16   MATCH

vertex_bone_weights is (13718, 9), nine influences per vertex. An earlier cost estimate assumed four and is low by roughly 2x: the mesh forward is about 1.5 MMAC, not 0.7.

RFD 1126’s decision clamps every unrolled step to the Kusudama cone. How that clamp is BUILT was settled in a meeting, and it is not the obvious reading of the phrase.
No kusudama carries two or more cones. Constraints are pairwise, and concatenated. A joint limit that a multi-cone kusudama was being asked to express is built instead as a concatenation of pairwise ones, and nothing in the pipeline constructs a kusudama of two or more rotation cones.
Note the rule is stricter than the measurement below requires. The degeneracy was measured at three equidistant cones; the rule cuts at two. That margin is deliberate rather than an overstatement of the evidence: two cones already admit the opposed case, whose centre sum is degenerate for the same reason, and a threshold nobody has to reason about at the call site is worth more than the one cone it gives up.
The measurement behind that choice is already in humanoid-rom/FINDINGS.md:
3 equidistant cones, 120 degrees apart    |sum| = 4.003e-16   degenerate
KusudamaSolver derived the pole of its gnomonic projection by summing every cone centre and normalising. Three equidistant cones sum to zero, normalize of zero is undefined, and one unit in the last place moves the derived pole by 45 degrees. The flip is a degenerate centroid and not a race. KusudamaEncoding.lean separately retires the pole derivation in favour of projecting against the nearest cone, which is a fix to the solver; the decision recorded here is upstream of it, and removes the many-cone case from the pipeline rather than repairing it.
The consequence for an unrolled clamp is favourable. A pairwise kusudama is a fixed, small computation, and a concatenation of them is a fixed-length chain of the same, so the whole constraint stays feed-forward with no data-dependent count. Comparisons and selects are Min and Where, which the backbone already compiled. A many-cone kusudama would have needed a normalise whose input can be zero, and an INT8 pipeline has no good answer for that division.
Recorded because the unrolled clamp is a new consumer of this decision, and building a single multi-cone kusudama is what reads most naturally from “clamp to the Kusudama cone”.



Utilisation, which every throughput number above assumes. Whether the unrolled fit reaches an acceptable residual as a percentage of stature at the precision the part offers, which is the number the whole approach rests on. Rig calibration, which nothing in the workspace solves. The cost of two compiled graphs and a per-frame context switch on one device.

text: A first pass counted MACs from the ONNX graph and reported num_windows=1 as CHEAPER, at 0.83x. That number is wrong. title: Logbook: what an edge NPU takes, and what the ANNY forward will not export
text:
The first error the DFC reports is IndexError: list index out of range inside LayerNorm axis mapping, from an empty input_format. Three explanations were proposed and each was tested with a minimal reproduction:
rank-3 LayerNorm alone            PARSE OK
window reshape then LayerNorm     PARSE OK
CLS concat producing 577 tokens   PARSE OK
All three pass in isolation and fail inside the real graph. Format inference is whole-graph, so a toy that parses proves nothing. The honest error appears only when end_node_names is passed, and it names Tile: unsupported concat over axis batch. The IndexError is a downstream symptom of the simplify-and-retry path.
Hailo’s own Model Zoo settles the CLS question independently: it ships timm ViTs and parses them whole with no start or end node overrides, and ViT-Base is 197 tokens, which is prime.

text:
825 ONNX nodes become 336 Hailo layers. Clipped to rf-detr-cpp/docs/measurements/hailo10h-backbone-576-nw1.hn.zst, 6 KB.
130 normalization   65 conv   46 layer_normalization   25 ew_add
 24 matmul          14 feature_splitter   12 softmax    4 concat
layer_normalization compiles 46 times and concat 4 times, so neither is unsupported. Only concat over the batch axis is, which is what windowing produces.
The HAR itself is 102.5 MB and is not kept. 101.4 MB of it is windows_1.npz, weights that duplicate a checkpoint already held. zstd compresses the whole HAR by 8.5% and -19 is no better than -3, because float32 weights are near entropy. The .hn compresses 41.8x.

text:
Whole model, num_windows=1, backbone plus a plain-DETR decoder, at 30% utilisation:
res    tokens    GMAC   INT8    INT4
288       576    17.8   168f    337f
336       784    25.8   139f    279f
384      1024    35.9    84f    167f
432      1296    48.7    62f    123f

1280 is not reachable: the keypoint variant is patch 12 with 2 windows, so resolution must divide by 24, and 1280 does not. AssertionError: Backbone requires input shape to be divisible by 24. The 12xx options are 1200, 1224, 1248, 1272, 1296.
Four cameras at 432 and 120 fps needs 117% of one part at PERFECT utilisation. Asymmetric fits: three body cameras at 288 with one face camera at 432, 120 fps, is 61%.
Framing sets precision, not resolution. Feature stride is 12 input pixels, so at 432 a 1.7 m subject filling the frame gives 47 mm, about a golf ball, while a 200 mm face filling a dedicated camera gives 5.6 mm, about a pencil. 45x from framing alone.

title: DFC parse-bisect methodology, from an rf-detr investigation
text:
Recording the methodology two probes converged on today while task #64 tried to place the DFC-vs-rf-detr failure. Journal shape rather than an RFD; the finding is a pattern next probes can copy, not a decision.


When DFC’s ClientRunner.translate_onnx_model rejects a graph, the pair of errors that surfaces localizes different parts of the failure:

ValueError: channels is not in list (from onnx_translator/onnx_graph.py:444, update_reshape_output_format calling input_format.index(Dims.CHANNELS)) means a Reshape node received a tensor with a format the tracker cannot map to NCHW. Usually fires downstream of an NLD-shaped (sequence) tensor being rewrapped as spatial.
IndexError: list index out of range from _convert_axes_to_nhwc at onnx_graph.py:2463 (input_format[axis]) means a LayerNormalization node’s axes attribute references a position beyond what DFC’s format tracker knows. Fires under the simplifier-retry pass. If a first-attempt channels is not in list and a simplifier-retry IndexError come out of the same run, they name two symptoms of the same LayerNormalization mishandling.

The retry pass ships [info] Simplified ONNX model for a parsing retry attempt (completion time: MM:SS.ss) and saves <model>.sim.onnx. Many minimal repros pass on the retry that fail on the first attempt, which is how a small negative control can accidentally read as green while the real model stays red.



The point is to isolate the failing site by parsing subgraphs, not the whole model. Two techniques, one wrong-then-right one right-from-the-start:
start_node_names + end_node_names on the full ONNX. Cheap because DFC does the extraction. Takes NODE names, not tensor names. A first probe using <node>_output_0 tensor names returned MisspellNodeError: Unable to find end node name, silently succeeding on the parser side while returning nothing useful. Once switched to bare node names (.name attribute on onnx.NodeProto, drop the _output_0), the partial parses land.
onnx.utils.extract_model(src, dst, inputs, outputs). Extracts a subgraph as a standalone ONNX file. Takes TENSOR names (which the caller maps as new graph inputs and outputs), not node names. Then run translate_onnx_model on the extracted file the same way. Slower per probe (writes an intermediate ONNX) but sidesteps DFC’s own extraction path, so it isolates the failure from any surprise-behavior of the partial-parse machinery.
Under start_node_names/end_node_names, DFC still walks the ancestors of the requested end nodes. So a cut ending inside the encoder still requires the encoder’s context and can fail during output-layer construction on a raw NLD tensor with IndexError: list index out of range. That error at an encoder-internal cut is not the actual failure site; it is DFC unable to emit a valid output on a tensor whose format is not NCHW. extract_model does not have this problem because the extracted subgraph’s inputs and outputs become the new graph’s boundary, so DFC has no encoder-side context to walk.



start_node_names/end_node_names is fast and useful for the “does this part fail” question against the whole model. onnx.utils.extract_model is right for the “is the failure in this component alone” question. Confusing the two costs a rewind: the first finding today read end_node_names=projector_end → ValueError: channels is not in list and concluded the projector was the failure site, but the same site when extracted (with the encoder cut off entirely) parsed green. The actual failure was the encoder outputs feeding the projector, and the end_node_names cut ran the whole encoder up to the projector boundary.



DFC’s simplifier retry can transform a Transpose → LayerNormalization → Transpose sequence into an atomic LN that DFC’s channel tracker accepts. A minimal PyTorch reproducer that ships with the same transpose-wrap pattern will therefore pass on the retry, even when the whole model with the same pattern fails. Two ways the minimal repro can miss the real failure:

The simplifier reduces the minimal repro but not the whole graph (because the whole graph has entangled Concat/Split/residual context the simplifier cannot fold).
The minimal repro’s LN operates on a tensor rank the tracker can map, while the whole graph’s LN operates on a tensor rank that trips _convert_axes_to_nhwc.

If the goal is a controlled negative test, extract the failing subgraph literally rather than reconstruct it in PyTorch. The extract preserves the axes, opset, and simplifier-boundary the whole model has.



A green partial parse always reports PARSE OK and saves a HAR under the name passed to save_har. A red partial parse hits an exception; the type(exc).__name__ + str(exc)[:400] is enough to distinguish MisspellNodeError (methodology bug), ValueError: channels is not in list (format tracker on Reshape), IndexError: list index out of range (format tracker on LN axes), and the shape-mismatch broadcast errors that fire when net_input_shapes overrides a static ONNX input to a resolution its position embeddings cannot span.
Rule 3 corollary: a probe that catches the exception and returns ok = False without naming the error type is decoration. Log the type and truncated message; save the traceback separately when the error class is genuinely surprising.



External sources touched during the investigation are in logbook-rfd-2199-hailo-int4-survey.md. The prototype scripts live in this session’s scratchpad under AppData/Local/Temp/.../scratchpad/dfc-compat/ (probe_seg2.py for resolution scan, probe_seg3_bisect.py for the wrong tensor-name bisect, probe_seg4_bisect.py for the corrected node-name bisect, extract_projector.py and extract_encoder.py for extract_model isolation). Not shipped; the pattern is what matters.

title: Logbook: CineForm in Godot, and what recording actually costs
text:
Apparatus: scripts/cfhd_probe.py for the codec precision, and v-sekai-fabric/entities-godot branch feat/movie-writer-async-readback for the rest. Measured on the local 4090 with a 16 thread CPU.


CineForm is a wavelet codec sold as visually lossless. Depth is a measurement in metres, so “you cannot see the difference” is not the test. Over 24 frames at 1024x1024 of a depth ramp carrying a 0.2 m step, because wavelets do their worst at edges:











pixel format

MB per 1000 frames

codec only




gbrp12le
12

Quantisation alone is 0.39 mm for each step at 12 bit and 1.56 mm at 10 bit, so CineForm adds about one step and no more. 0.46 mm is half a credit card’s thickness. 10 bit is ruled out: its 2.10 mm is coarser than the 0.54 mm agreement measured between two independent renderers, so it would become the largest error in the chain.
Retracted. A first probe reported 97% of codes bit exact and 0.0 mm from the codec. The probe clipped the depth step below the near plane, and flat clipped regions compress exactly, so the codec looked perfect on data that was already ruined. A check that passes on broken input certifies the defect.



No PQ, no HLG, no BT.2020, no SMPTE 2084 anywhere in the SDK. TAG_COLORSPACE_YUV knows 601 and 709 only. Its answer to dynamic range is the film scan one: log encode into 12 bits and record the curve so a decoder can invert it. That is latitude, not HDR10.
W13A and WP13, signed 16 bit with the whitepoint at 1<<13, look like the right answer and are not usable: CSampleEncoder::GetInputFormats does not advertise either. They appear only in VideoBuffers.cpp pitch arithmetic. The encoder’s first preference is RG64, 16 bit RGBA. The 8 bit BGRA this writer uses sits eleventh.



Five frictions, none visible from reading the code:

Godot builds with /fp:strict, under which MSVC’s C compiler does not fold floating point constant expressions, so the codec’s static colour matrices fail with C2099.
CoCreateGuid is reached only through platform branches that skip this configuration.
LPTSTR lpValueName takes a string literal. That is const correctness in C++, not the UNICODE mismatch it resembles, and undefining UNICODE would have “fixed” it by silently switching every Win32 call in the file to ANSI.
Five MessageBox calls raise a system modal licensing dialog from inside the encoder. In a headless render that blocks forever, and in a shipped game it cannot be dismissed.

CineForm is a wavelet codec sold as visually lossless. Depth is a measurement in metres, so “you cannot see the difference” is not the test. Over 24 frames at 1024x1024 of a depth ramp carrying a 0.2 m step, because wavelets do their worst at edges:

Quantisation alone is 0.39 mm for each step at 12 bit and 1.56 mm at 10 bit, so CineForm adds about one step and no more. 0.46 mm is half a credit card’s thickness. 10 bit is ruled out: its 2.10 mm is coarser than the 0.54 mm agreement measured between two independent renderers, so it would become the largest error in the chain.
Retracted. A first probe reported 97% of codes bit exact and 0.0 mm from the codec. The probe clipped the depth step below the near plane, and flat clipped regions compress exactly, so the codec looked perfect on data that was already ruined. A check that passes on broken input certifies the defect.

title: Logbook: CineForm in Godot, and what recording actually costs
text:
No PQ, no HLG, no BT.2020, no SMPTE 2084 anywhere in the SDK. TAG_COLORSPACE_YUV knows 601 and 709 only. Its answer to dynamic range is the film scan one: log encode into 12 bits and record the curve so a decoder can invert it. That is latitude, not HDR10.
W13A and WP13, signed 16 bit with the whitepoint at 1<<13, look like the right answer and are not usable: CSampleEncoder::GetInputFormats does not advertise either. They appear only in VideoBuffers.cpp pitch arithmetic. The encoder’s first preference is RG64, 16 bit RGBA. The 8 bit BGRA this writer uses sits eleventh.

title: Logbook: revoking a Bao cert-auth identity when the entry is a shared wildcard
text:
Date: 2026-09-03 Session: MPS (mps-45994b.agents.weftspun) Related: RFD 2195 (Bao Tailscale sidecar; Revocation section)


MPS-Dataset session (mps-dataset-68764.agents.weftspun) was revoked by operator instruction. Its cert authenticated through the shared auth/cert/certs/agents-weftspun entry, which had allowed_common_names=*.agents.weftspun and covered CUDA too. So the revocation had to remove one CN without dropping the entry.



bao write pki/revoke serial_number=<X> recorded the revocation in the PKI store and emitted error building CRLs: x509: issuer certificate doesn't contain a subject key identifier — a bao intermediate config issue, but also irrelevant here: the cert-auth method does not consult the CRL by default. A revoked cert still authenticates.



Three steps, in this order:

Read the current auth/cert/certs/agents-weftspun, preserve the certificate, token_policies, token_ttl, token_max_ttl, display_name fields, replace allowed_common_names with an explicit list that excludes the revoked CN. Write it back.
bao kv metadata delete agents/<revoked-cn> — remove the coordination-store row so peers don’t see a stale identity.
Update the 1Password item: annotate REVOKED 2026-09-03 with the reason, keep the cert body for audit.

Effective immediately. No CRL, no reload, no restart. pki/revoke on the serial(s) still runs alongside for the audit trail even though cert-auth ignores it.



The shared-wildcard case is the interesting one; the per-CN case is easier and covered in the RFD 2195 runbook. This entry exists to name the extra step the wildcard case adds: preserve the entry, narrow the CN list, versus delete the entry.



Pattern shipped in RFD 2195 DETAILS’s Revocation section. Next revocation should follow that; this entry stays as the event that produced it.
This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

title: V-Sekai Multiplayer Fabric Deck Log — 2026-09-01 (Tuesday)
text:
Date: 2026-09-01
The weftspun-fdb cluster, the openbao instance on top of it, the spot broker, and the chibifire.com app were gone from Fly at start of day. Tigris weftspun-fdb-blob and R2 weftspun-fdb-dr had both survived, so the day was running RFD 2143’s DR runbook against the case that RFD had partially anticipated — compute lost, storage kept. The runbook had called itself theatre as of 2026-08-31 because RFD 2141’s break-glass CA was not in 1Password; this run landed that CA at DR-time and the theatre note is retired.
The R2 snapshot described restorable, 0.19 days old, 99 644 bytes — RFD 2143’s 2026-08-31 measurement had put the cluster at Sum of key-value sizes = 0 MB, so 100 KB agrees: this is Bao’s PKI mount metadata and internal system tables. The fdbrestore -w from R2 into the fresh single-node TLS cluster is running as this entry is written.



RFD 2144, which records the first run of RFD 2143’s DR runbook against a real disaster and lands the break-glass CA RFD 2141 named as its own prerequisite. op://Personal/FDB-CA/{cert,key} now holds a P-384 self-signed root and its private key, from which the recovered cluster’s machine leaves are minted; RFD 2141’s phases 2–3 will rotate them to certificates signed by the CA Bao’s PKI mount holds, once Bao is unsealed against the restored FDB.
logbook-rfd2144-dr-runbook-first-run.md, which captures the five inline defects the runbook did not name — no home for WEFT_FDB_CLUSTER_ID, Bao secrets in notesPlain, Fly storage create refusing an existing bucket, health checks fail-closed on first deploy, and zsh read -p silent in the AI session’s ! context — plus the T+ timeline as it is measured.
weftspun-fdb cluster id in 1Password, holding the freshly minted WEFT_FDB_CLUSTER_ID. The runbook now reads this rather than assuming any prior copy exists.





weftspun-fdb is a new Fly app with new coordinator addresses and a new cluster ID. Clients’ cluster files change to weft:<newid>@<newcoords>. Coordinator addresses change on any rebuild anyway, so the identity change costs nothing extra to consume.
The cluster runs at WEFT_FDB_MACHINES=1 and WEFT_FDB_REDUNDANCY=single while the restore runs and Bao comes back up. RFD 2143 wants three at double before real writes; that scale-up is scheduled after Bao unseals and the machine leaves are rotated to the restored CA.
The R2 S3 access key weftspun-fdb-dr s3 in 1P was used to bootstrap the restore. It rotates and revokes at end of DR, per RFD 2143 step 8, with the replacement key going into Bao once Bao is back.





RFD 2143’s “the runbook is theatre” line, which had held since 2026-08-31. RFD 2141’s prerequisite — the break-glass CA in 1P — landed in passing during this DR, and the runbook then ran end-to-end.
fdb-entrypoint.sh in 6-datasource/store/fly/ gated the [backup_agent] config block on Tigris credentials being set. An R2-only setup — precisely the DR path — spawned no backup agent, so fdbrestore queued forever. Now gates on $backup = 1 || $backup_r2 = 1, picks blob_credentials from whichever destination is wired, and both agents in [backup_agent] and [backup_agent.2] are fine to start whenever either destination is wired.
OpenBao’s Shamir sys/rekey/init and sys/generate-root/attempt endpoints return 405 / 404 by default; Vault registers them without a flag, OpenBao gates them on disable_unauthed_rekey_endpoints = false and disable_unauthed_generate_root_endpoints = false in the listener config (see internal/http/handler.go lines 174–192). service-openbao/config-fdb.hcl now sets both. bao operator rekey and bao operator generate-root now run.
The weftspun-bao root 1P item is now the single source of truth: password CONCEALED holds the rotated root token, unseal_key CONCEALED holds the rekeyed unseal key, notesPlain carries a status note only (no secrets). The three stale unseal-key copies (init doc, prior CONCEALED, notesPlain) are noted as stale in the item’s note. Three orphan root token accessors accumulated during rotation attempts and were revoked once generate-root came online.





RFD 2145: certificate lifetimes, from a risk-based ceiling. Replaces the 10-year CAs and 1-to-2-year leaves RFDs 2134, 2141, 2142, 2144 landed with. New ceilings: 25 years on the offline Root’s notAfter with 5-year policy rotation (X.509 makes notAfter mandatory per RFC 5280 §4.1.2.5, so the field must exist, but rotation is a policy commitment rather than a validation gate on an offline key that pays no rent), 3 years on intermediates with 1-year rotation, 90 days on mTLS service leaves with ≤45-day rotation, and 14 days on WebTransport leaves (Chromium’s serverCertificateHashes maximum). Citations live as .cff files under rfd/2145-certificate-lifetimes/references/ — RFC 5280, Mozilla Root Store Policy §7.1’s 15-year public-trust cap, CA/B Forum SC-081v3’s 200 → 100 → 47 day schedule, NCSC’s “as short as practical” principle, NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 §5.3.6 cryptoperiod framing, W3C WebTransport. RFDs 2134, 2141, 2142, 2144 carry in-place retractions pointing here for the specific numbers replaced. S2145 registered.





spot.chibifire.com — first custom domain wired to a recovered app. CF A + AAAA for the shared IPv4 and dedicated IPv6 Fly allocated to spot-broker, plus the ACME challenge CNAME and ownership TXT records; fly certs add then Issued in about a minute. https://spot.chibifire.com/ returns 200 with a Let’s Encrypt cert (issuer=Let's Encrypt CN=YE2).
Four secrets moved from 1P into Bao KV as source of truth (task 19): secret/weftspun/fdb/cluster-id, secret/weftspun/cloudflare/edit-zone-dns, secret/weftspun/cloudflare/r2-bearer, secret/weftspun/fdb/r2-dr. Each value tagged with its provenance. 1P items retained as offline mirror.
RFD 2146 — Bao is the secret store, cert-auth is the fence. Five policies (admin, dns-editor, fdb-config-reader, pki-issuer, app-reader-spot) and three initial cert-auth roles (admin-v2, spot-broker-app, fdb-cluster) each binding a specific chibifire.com Intermediate CA v2 leaf to the minimum policies it needs. Verified: cert-only DNS edit path (no op read) works end-to-end; negative controls (spot-broker-app and fdb-cluster attempting to read cloudflare/edit-zone-dns) both return 403 permission denied. RFD 2142 promoted from prediscussion to discussion and points forward here for the role table. S2146 registered.
logbook/logbook-rfd2146-zerotrust-roles-first-run.md — measured cost of enabling cert-auth (~9 HTTP POSTs, no Bao restart needed), the leaf-vs-bundle finding on TLS chain construction, and the two negative controls.





weftspun-fdb restored, scaled to 3 machines under double redundancy, fault tolerance = 1 zone, every leaf signed by the restored chibifire.com Intermediate CA, break-glass CA retired from live trust and kept in 1P as FDB-CA cert/FDB-CA key for the next DR.
weftspun-bao restored on FDB, PKI mount reappeared with both issuers, both mTLS parties on the root chain, root token and unseal key rotated.
R2 keys stored in Bao at secret/weftspun-fdb/r2-dr as the source of truth; the dashboard-side rotation (Cloudflare’s public API does not expose R2 S3 key creation) is queued as a followup.
spot-broker and chibifire-com were parked; recreating them from their fly.toml files with fresh Bao-issued client certs is the resume-work.

Citations live as .cff files under rfd/2145-certificate-lifetimes/references/ — RFC 5280, Mozilla Root Store Policy §7.1’s 15-year public-trust cap, CA/B Forum SC-081v3’s 200 → 100 → 47 day schedule, NCSC’s “as short as practical” principle, NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 §5.3.6 cryptoperiod framing, W3C WebTransport. RFDs 2134, 2141, 2142, 2144 carry in-place retractions pointing here for the specific numbers replaced. S2145 registered.

title: V-Sekai Multiplayer Fabric Deck Log — 2026-08-07 (Friday)
text:
Date: 2026-08-07
Archived six repositories that the Fly.io move of rfd/0089 left without a consumer, and resynchronized the organization inventory in rfd/0062 to the real organization. The inventory had drifted far enough to name ten repositories by names they no longer carry, to list five repositories that left the organization, and to omit about thirty that exist.
The sweep also surfaced one inconsistency that no record explains: zone-server-h2o is archived on GitHub while rfd/0094 names it the host of the minimum user-generated-content game loop.



RFD 2105, which archives the self-host-era support repositories and the empty stubs: fabric-container-verify, the rfd/0056 quadlet verification queue, whose every target rfd/0089 already archived; fabric-casync-central, which never carried content; fabric-scoop-central, the scoop bucket for the Windows demo of the parked godot-loop-slice; fabric-platform-central, the rfd/0065 Burrito and casync packaging path; and the two empty placeholders vulkan-video-godot and steamdeck. Each one is tombstoned rather than deleted, so its history stays reachable.
A record of the fabric-platform-central risk in that RFD’s DETAILS.md. rfd/0090 describes a live Burrito release of uro on Fly.io, and rfd/0065 puts that packaging in the archived repository. One API call reverses the archive if the deploy still reads from it.
A Moved to V-Sekai-archive section in the rfd/0062 inventory, for the three repositories that left this organization: lean-predictive-bvh, viser, and usd-converter-for-vrchat.
Counts in the inventory: 72 repositories, 48 active and 24 archived.





The rfd/0062 inventory now uses current repository names, per rfd/0064. GitHub keeps a redirect after a rename, so every old name still resolved and hid the drift. godot is fabric-godot-core, merge is fabric-godot-assembly, observability is fabric-game-observability, manuals is multiplayer-fabric-manuals, and the five *-image repositories are the *-quadlet repositories. rfd/0105’s DETAILS.md carries the full mapping.
The inventory’s repository sections follow the current stack: an engine and client area, a zone host and guests area for rfd/0094’s composition, a backend and data area for the FoundationDB work of rfd/0103, one hexagon-cores area holding both the canonical hexagons and the standalone Lean workspaces, and a content flow and authoring area.
The archived table now carries a Basis column naming the decision that retired each repository, and lists all 24 rather than 3.





The inventory’s service-images section. Every repository it listed is archived by rfd/0089, which supersedes rfd/0061’s quadlet deployment target.




Created multiplayer-fabric-archive and moved every retired record there, per RFD 2106: the 26 rejected and superseded MADR records under _archive/decisions/, the image they cite, and the two superseded RFDs, rfd/0011 on the observability stack and rfd/0061 on the deployment target. The new repository carries the manuals history up to the split, so each moved file keeps every commit that touched it at its original path. It holds plain Markdown, with no site and no checks.
Both superseded RFDs used to render as current. A reader who opened either one read a dead design with no marking on the page.
Repairing the inbound links was the work a move forces, because a deleted file with no stub leaves a 404 on the site. Four relative links in the 2026-06-06 deck log, two pointers in rfd/0071, and one reference each in rfd/0089, rfd/0060, rfd/0070, and the rfd/0062 inventory now point at the archive repository. _quarto.yml drops the decisions/attachments resource.
The move also exposed a link that never resolved. Two archived records cite the debug-orb image relative to _archive/decisions/, and the image sat two directories away in decisions/attachments/. Quarto skips _archive, so no rendered page ever exercised it. The archive repository puts the image where the existing links expect it.




The asset-citation guidance named references.bib, a file the repository no longer carries. The bibliography converted to CFF, and pages/references.qmd renders the 94 entries under references: in CITATION.cff through cffconvert. AGENTS.md and rfd/0013 now name CITATION.cff. The changelog entries that describe references.bib stay as they are, because they record what was true on their own date.
The site config pointed at the pre-rename repository. site-url read .../github.io/manuals and repo-url read .../v-sekai-multiplayer-fabric/manuals, while the site publishes at .../multiplayer-fabric-manuals/, so every edit-this-page link and the feed URL resolved to the wrong place. Both now name the current repository, as do the three gh api .../rulesets commands in rfd/0021.




zone-server-h2o was archived and is unarchived again. It is the host repository, and RFD 2107 records the tier around it: h2o as HTTP ingress and reverse proxy, Janet as the dynamic layer for routing glue and configuration, libtaskweft as a C library holding HTN search and game state, and Godot as the client over GDExtension. Janet loads the C core as a native module. Rust is out, so the core is C.
FoundationDB stays the store, through libfdb_c. rfd/0075 stands and rfd/0006’s CockroachDB does not describe this tier, so the FDB record set stays in force: rfd/0002, rfd/0073, rfd/0074, rfd/0084, rfd/0097, and rfd/0103. ecto_foundationdb and ecto-bench-tpcc keep a live consumer.
The record states its own gaps rather than guessing past them. The startup, memory and speed claims for this tier are not measured, and data/measurements/ holds nothing for Janet or a C taskweft core. Four questions stay open: which part drives the libfdb_c callbacks, where Elixir and zone-backend sit, whether Janet replaces the libriscv guest runtime, and which part terminates a WebTransport session.



RFD 2108 makes a simulation guest a local shared object loaded over the plain C ABI, and h2o routes to it with no network hop. The CDN keeps one job, which is bulk asset delivery, and it no longer delivers guest programs for simulation.
Fan-out runs inside the tick. One publish ring per zone, one writer, and many readers holding cursors. The 100-byte packet of rfd/0053 is serialized once and fanned out as a pointer and a refcount, so N subscribers cost one serialization rather than N. A cross-loop delivery takes one batched wakeup per tick, which caps a loop near 64 wakeups per second at 64 Hz.
FoundationDB stays off that path. rfd/0097 measured a watch fire at 12115.1 us, which is most of a 15.6 ms tick, against 8.9 us for an AF_UNIX round trip. The watch probe also failed at exactly 10000 watches with error 1032, and a watch is edge-triggered, so it loses values between the fire and the re-read. The tick owns the libfdb_c callback chain of rfd/0073 and appends the durable log off-tick.
The record states the cost of local mode rather than hiding it. A local .so shares the zone’s address space, so a guest fault takes the zone down. rfd/0083 chose Fil-C for memory safety and rfd/0095 built two guest classes for the same reason, and local mode has neither property. That suits first-party simulation code and does not suit user-generated code, so rfd/0094’s UGC loop needs its own record.
RFD 2108 closes two of RFD 2107’s four open questions, which are the database path owner and the guest boundary. Two stay open and one arrives: where Elixir and zone-backend sit, which part terminates a WebTransport session, and how a UGC guest runs.



RFD 2109 names egress as the cost that binds, and the store as the cost that does not. Bandwidth per client sets the bill, and one node serves the database load. No deployment runs, so the record carries no cost figure.
The tier count drops to two. Godot is the client, holding rendering, XR, IK, and local physics. Elixir and Phoenix form the server, holding identity, the room directory, and the presence relay. The server relays presence rather than simulating it, so Phoenix supplies the identity and sessions that a Godot server would need written in GDScript.
The store stays FoundationDB, through ecto_foundationdb, so rfd/0075 stands. The record accepts rfd/0103’s limits rather than working around them: no joins, no or, no aggregates in the database, and one Between clause per query. That trade holds because the relational need is analytical, and the analytical half runs on zstd Parquet and DuckDB as data/measurements/ already does. OLTP access is point lookups by player and room identity.
Twelve stores are recorded with their outcome. TiDB, YDB, and Apache Ignite are viable and not chosen, and the record says why for each. TiDB is the one that keeps relational form with no adapter work, at the cost of more processes and MySQL’s weaker constraint set. Rust was banned and then unbanned during the search, which returned TiDB to the list. Rivet 2.0 is Apache 2.0 and ships a TypeScript SDK, with no Elixir or Godot client.
taskweft stays an Elixir NIF, which V-Sekai-fire/multiplayer-fabric-taskweft already is, so Janet and the C libtaskweft are dropped.
rfd/0107 and rfd/0108 are marked abandoned and carry a pointer to this record. Their measurements stay valid, and the back-pressure rule of rfd/0108 still applies to any relay.
Five questions stay open on record: player-hosted zones against server-hosted, interest management as the only lever on the 256 kbps figure, server authority that a relay cannot give, whether the Godot WebTransport client speaks to a Phoenix endpoint, and how many FoundationDB processes run and where.



RFD 2110 makes a zone a child process under Rivet’s container-runner, one process per room. The child is the engine at tag v2026.06.27.1907-multiplayer-fabric, which resolves to commit 2cecde75 and reports Godot 4.7.0 beta. That tag’s modules/ already carries sandbox for libriscv guests, http3 for WebTransport, multiplayer_fabric and multiplayer_fabric_asset for the zone, xr_grid for presence, and openxr with webxr for XR. So one build is the client, the zone server, and the guest host.
A C child of h2o plus libriscv stays possible and is not built. Its only advantage is memory per process, and that figure is unmeasured. No resonance module appears at the tag, so rfd/0022’s spatial audio needs checking before anyone relies on it.
One process per room deletes work rather than adding it. rfd/0072, rfd/0082, and rfd/0086 become unnecessary, because each exists only to hold many zones in one process. rfd/0080 narrows to one room’s entities. A guest fault kills one room rather than every room, which is what rfd/0095 wanted from Bubblewrap.
The actor input is four optional CBOR fields, read from container-runner/src/input.rs: command, args, env, and port. The decoded input is also the actor’s persisted state, so a woken actor restores the same launch spec, and unknown fields are ignored rather than rejected. A room’s scene and its tuning therefore travel in the actor input, and no zone-side registry is needed.
The transport is settled by the runner’s source rather than by its documentation. container-runner is TCP-only. src/proxy.rs forwards to http://127.0.0.1:{child_port} and the ws:// form, src/child.rs checks readiness with TcpStream::connect((Ipv4Addr::LOCALHOST, child_port)), and no udp, quic, http3, or h2 appears in the runner source. TCP_NODELAY does not appear either, so Nagle is unmitigated there.
The answer is two sockets in one child. A TCP port satisfies Rivet’s contract and carries the control plane. A UDP port carries game traffic outside Rivet’s tunnel, with the engine’s http3 picoquic module on it. Rivet never touches the pose stream, so rfd/0008, rfd/0023, rfd/0049, rfd/0058, and rfd/0088 all stand. The cost is that Rivet’s gateway does not route the UDP port, so a zone directory must publish the host and port, which makes the Uro role required rather than optional.

title: V-Sekai Multiplayer Fabric Deck Log — 2026-06-29 (Monday)
text:
Date: 2026-06-29
Trimmed the heavy decision records back to the lean MADR template, applying YAGNI to the docs. A decision record carries its context, decision, downsides, alternatives, and verification; the scoring ceremony around it added bulk without changing the decision, so it came out.
Then archived the standalone presence demo as superseded, and recorded the YAGNI principle as its own decision.



A decision record, YAGNI times structure to the need, adopting Beck’s framing of YAGNI as a question of timing, with Kent Beck’s essay added to CITATION.cff.





Six decision records dropped their CRIS score tables, Tags lists, Further Reading bibliographies, and the body Status and Decision Makers sections that only duplicated the YAML frontmatter, and collapsed The Road Not Taken to one line per alternative: maglev cycle 1 gateway handshake, loot-action core-loop MVP vertical slice, fabric-platform-central as Elixir OTP app, game-loop-first delivery sequence, release tag progression, and sccache GitHub Actions cache. The maglev record kept its round-trip verification evidence under a Confirmation heading. The frontmatter and the decisions index are unchanged.
The MADR proposal template follows the same lean shape, with status and decision-makers in frontmatter, so new records keep to the load-bearing sections.
The loot-action MVP vertical slice gained a Confirmation section recording the verified as-built state against its decided scope: two of five cores wired (combat and loot), SQLite without a CockroachDB adapter, no performance-gate enforcement, and an OpenXR preset that duplicates the Windows build. The runtime smoke result is not yet recorded.





The standalone presence demo moved to _archive/decisions/, marked superseded by the loot-action vertical slice: the ghostly partial-body avatar, the cold-boot dependencies, the pose networking, and the orb presence markers. Their orb sibling was already archived. Three live records that linked to them were delinked so the rendered site keeps no dead links.

title: V-Sekai Multiplayer Fabric Deck Log — 2026-06-12 (Friday)
text:
Date: 2026-06-12
Recorded the instanced loot-action core-loop slice as MADRs: the product scope and the performance gate, the five hexagons, and the core architecture around Lean kernels lowered to SPIR-V over r128 fixed-point.



Product and process decisions: MVP vertical slice, first-party content budgets, genre-generic naming, CASSIE desktop authoring, and a merged build via the editor MCP.
Hexagon decisions (core, ports, adapters): combat, loot, progression, budgeter, and presence, the last wrapping the existing presence decisions.
Core architecture decisions: Lean kernel cores with flat-C adapters, Lean to Slang to SPIR-V codegen, r128 fixed-point as a Lean library, the pure-reducer byte-state contract, deterministic state, server authority with deferred rollback, sandboxed RISC-V behavior, the forward renderer, and the webtransportd transport adapter.





The merged multiplayer-fabric assembly builds: the linux double-precision editor (23 branches, zero conflicts) and the Android arm64 double template (android_release.apk), per the toolchain decision.
Wire parity under server authority in the merged build: loot (256 rolls), combat (88 effects), and four-player contention (64 rounds, 4 concurrent clients) all match their Lean golden vectors; headless OpenXR initializes against Monado per the Monado decision.
New repos: loot, combat, progression (each a core/ports/adapters triad with Plausible-pinned golden vectors), and fabric-verify (the smokes as a quadlet queue, per the queue decision).
The r128 chain: the Lean R128 matches the vendored r128.c (8,200 vectors x 7 ops), the uint32-limb R128L matches R128 (50,000 sweep), and the lean-slang-emitted SPIR-V kernel matches r128.c on the GPU (4,096 multiplies), per the r128 Lean library decision.
lean-slang runs on Lean 4.30 (V-Sekai-fire/lean-slang#1).





merge gitassembly drops the dead feat/spatial-audio-server ref (merge#36), so the canonical assembly runs again.
The http3 listener findings are recorded as a decision: one listener per process, reply routing to a single session, and a teardown double free, with the loop’s interim shape until the module fixes land.





The http3 multi-session reply routing and teardown double free, as godot#56 — the fix pattern comes from the webtransportd single-pending-slot bug (fire/webtransportd@f0fc9a4). Post-fix, four concurrent clients each receive their own winner announcements and the server survives teardown; the quadlet four-player smoke verifies per client.





The entity-transform wire is integral: int64 absolute micrometers (no origin shift), velocity tied to the predictive BVH’s V_MAX, a 42-byte payload, and a Lean+Plausible source-of-truth in entity_packet (decision, godot#58).
Fabric channels are reliability classes with control in the packet payload (decision).
The MCP runtime bridge drives the deployed OpenXR build over adb (decision, vsekai-godot-mcp#1).
New repos: the standalone Lean workspaces loot-core, combat-core, progression-core, and the playable loop-slice.





The picoquic WebTransport server survives four or more concurrent sessions and completes full rounds, on feat/module-http3. Reliable traffic rides one persistent framed stream per session instead of a fresh stream per message, which exhausts stream credit and starves the connect handshake (decision). Five supporting fixes hold the network thread up under load: a mutex on the inbound queue, an inclusive wake-loop that drains and services receive on every callback, get_packet_peer peeking the queue front per the MultiplayerPeer contract, a connection table sized for the fanout, and the picoquic textlog gated behind the verbose flag.
The queue race and the wake-loop starvation each carry a Lean+Plausible proof in the new http3-queue workspace: the locked queue stays size-honest for every schedule, the inclusive loop stays starvation-free, and the models exhibit the schedules the unlocked and exclusive variants fail.





The loop chooses its transport at launch through TRANSPORT: ENet for the local slice, WebTransport for the browser and headset paths, with the text protocol unchanged across both. Control rides reliable on channel 0, the high-rate transform rides unreliable on channel 1.
An OpenXR client joins the four-player loop over LAN as a real player: it autoconnects to the desktop server, fights in immersive OpenXR above the frame floor, and the round commits progression. The headset controllers drive the loop through polled, edge-detected actions (left thumbstick locomotion, right trigger attack, right A grab, left Y teleport vote), reading the bool action trigger_click rather than a float trigger, with the XR camera held by reference so the locomotion branch runs.
The merge assembler returns to the base branch and drops the local assembly branch on every run, including dry runs and failures, so a half-built assembly leaves the checkout clean.

title: Weftspun RFDs
text:
OID: urn:oid:1.3.6.1.4.1.66606.1.1.1175
State: discussion Flight level: L3


One native binary produces both demos:

Game demo (interactive). A native window on the operator’s desktop opens the Starforged decision-point VN. The player IS the caller; the VRM portrait is the interlocutor; a planner supplies the legal moves for each decision point.
Video demo (headless capture). The same binary run as --headless --write-movie captures the scene per shot; the encoder is CineForm (ffmpeg blocklisted, see memory [[ffmpeg-blocklisted]]).

Same source tree, same binary, same .tscn / .tres assets, one invocation flag distinguishes the heads. The video is what the game looks like when you run it deterministically over a shot list.



Godot as the runtime, Vulkan as the renderer, ggml for inference, CineForm for the encoder. Concrete implementation lands as commits in the respective repos when the work is done, not as forward- looking RFDs.
This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

Split the lean-predictive-bvh proof monorepo into one repository per hexagon cluster, along the dependency seams the lakefile already drew, and archived the monorepo. Updated the vertical-slice repository map to match.



Six standalone Lean workspaces, one per hexagon cluster, each carrying its own core/ports/adapters tree, a lakefile that wires its siblings over require ... from git, and a CI gate that builds the production closure: lean-shared-core, the dependency-free primitive types every other core requires; lean-rebac-core, the NoGod / ReBAC authorization core; lean-spatial-oracle, the predictive BVH and its R128 fixed-point with ghost expansion, SAH, and Hilbert broadphase, emitting predictive_bvh.h through the AmoLean codegen; lean-humanoid-rom, range-of-motion and IK constraints with the body-model and biomechanics citations; lean-fabric-protocol, the networking and SLA proofs (saturation, waypoint bounds, abyssal SLA); and lean-interest-mgmt, authority-interest and solve-order. The push order follows the dependency graph: shared-core and rebac-core first, then spatial-oracle, then fabric-protocol, then interest-mgmt, and each repository’s lake build is green.





The repository map lists the predictive-oracle proofs as the six per-cluster repositories above, replacing the single lean-predictive-bvh entry under the wire, transport, and determinism specs.

title: V-Sekai Multiplayer Fabric Deck Log — 2026-06-30 (Tuesday)
text:
Date: 2026-06-30
Made the loot-action slice runnable on a bare Windows 11 machine, with no Docker and no WSL. The slice now ships as a downloadable release: the authoritative server, the client, and the bots that fill the four-player party are native Windows executables, persistence is in-process SQLite, and an optional native observability stack (VictoriaMetrics + OpenTelemetry) runs alongside. One double-click on run-demo.cmd starts the whole thing.
Along the way the loop closed its last gap — the loot a player wins now travels back to the client and shows in the hub — and the Windows build and packaging were hardened across several release cuts, v0.1.0-dev.3 through v0.1.0-dev.6.



A native Windows demo of the godot-loop-slice vertical slice, on the v0.1.0-dev.6 release: a plain-exe …-demo-windows.zip plus three unsigned MSI installers — the all-in-one demo, a server-only install (binds all interfaces and prints the host’s LAN address), and a client-only install (connects to a given server address).
Double-click .cmd launchers (run-demo.cmd, run-server.cmd, run-client.cmd) that run the PowerShell launcher as an in-memory scriptblock, so Windows execution policy and Mark-of-the-Web never block a downloaded script — no scoop and no policy change. The MSI Start-menu shortcuts point at the same launchers.

title: V-Sekai Multiplayer Fabric Deck Log — 2026-08-17 (Monday)
text:
Date: 2026-08-17
The WebTransport contract has a second implementation, and it contradicted one claim the fabric makes about its own wire before carrying a byte of real traffic. transport-fanout caps a subscriber’s slice at 64 records and calls 6400 bytes “comfortably inside one message”; two stacks that share no code both put the limit at 11 records, and datasource-queen’s own WT_MTU_MAX agrees with them rather than with the comment.
That is one finding rather than a pile, and the count is worth keeping honest. Building the pair also cost three library defects — an EC key pywebtransport would not load, an iceoryx2 subscriber buffer that drops the oldest of three sends, and an aioquic datagram queue that wedges on an oversized send. Those are real and none of them says anything about the contract.



RFD 2123, which puts a second implementation of the WebTransport contract on a stack sharing no code with the first. RFD 2088 chose one QUIC stack on both ends, which buys interoperability by construction and gives up the check: a wire implemented once describes the program that implements it. Khronos ratifies against two independent implementations for the same reason.
transport-gateway-python, the reliable half on aioquic 1.3.0, and transport-ingest-python, the datagram half. Both hand off over the iceoryx2 ring through the prebuilt wheel, and both carry no player traffic. aioquic implements QUIC and TLS 1.3 in Python from the RFCs, so it shares no code with the picoquic the C pair vendors. Binding picoquic from Python was rejected because both ends would then run the same QUIC and the same TLS, and h2o because its WebTransport is an unmerged pull request against an HTTP/3 stack h2o calls experimental.
A Python emitter in contract-entity-packet, so lake exe packet_emit writes the C header, the Python codec and the 64 golden vectors from one run. A second implementation that retyped the layout would test whether two people can copy a table. Regenerating the header and the vectors produced byte-identical output, so the change perturbs nothing.
A conformance gate in both new repositories: 64 vectors decoded, re-encoded and compared byte for byte, with a --self-test that corrupts one vector and must fail. CI runs both on every pull request and in the merge group.





transport-gateway is transport-gateway-c and transport-ingest is transport-ingest-c. Two implementations of one contract are distinguished only by how they are built, so RFD 2111’s preference for names that say what a thing does cannot separate them. Naming the language rather than the library survives a change of library, which this day already exercised: the Python pair moved from pywebtransport to aioquic before it merged and neither name moved. Neither pair keeps the unqualified name, because the unqualified name implies the other is a variant. transport-picoquic is the precedent.
The GitHub descriptions on both C repositories. Each read “hands the result to a plane over iceoryx2”, a word RFD 2111 retired in favour of interactor. The READMEs were converted and the descriptions were missed.
The rfd/0062 inventory gains a transport-layers section, which it had none of, and its counts move from 73 repositories and 49 active to 75 and 51.
The manifest count in fabric’s README moves from 45 projects to 47. That count is gated, and the gate’s own negative control hard-codes the number, so the control had to move with it or it would certify nothing.





Eight stale repository references in six files across five repositories, each in its own pull request: transport-fanout, transport-gateway-c, transport-ingest-c, interactor-ward, entities-gyre and datasource-queen. check_docs.py’s moved-repository check found every one of them; GitHub’s redirects meant nothing was broken, and a name that no longer says which of two implementations it means is the problem.
A burst of ring publishes lost its oldest sample. iceoryx2 defaults a subscriber’s buffer to 2 with safe overflow on, so three records published back to back arrived as two. Both repositories now set the buffer explicitly and keep safe overflow, because rfd/0108 requires that a lagging reader never stall the writer.




The live cross-test against the C pair is not written, and there is nothing to write it against. transport-gateway-c and transport-ingest-c have no main and no CMakeLists.txt, and both READMEs say “State: not started”. transport-ingest-c’s copy of the transport code is a stale fork of transport-gateway-c’s, passing an h3zero_callback_ctx_t where h3zero_callback casts to picohttp_server_parameters_t and missing the h3zero_declare_stream_prefix call. That divergence is why both Python repositories consume one emitted codec instead of two copies, and it is recorded in both OPEN_GAPS.md files that the shared conformance gate is itself duplicated with nothing checking that the copies agree.
A dropped ring sample stays undetectable. HeaderPublishSubscribe carries a node id, a publisher id and an element count, and no sequence number. rfd/0108 says a subscriber whose cursor falls out of the ring receives a resync signal rather than a gap; no such signal exists, and defining one is a wire decision rather than a transport one.

title: Logbook: the ANNY fit that the corpus does not need
text:
A day was spent making ANNY reproduce another body, and the pipeline never asked for that. The measurements are kept because three of them answer questions that outlived the goal, and the wrong turn is kept because a reader who knows which road is a dead end is better off than one who only knows the current answer.


The corpus pipeline is skeleton poses ANNY, Mitsuba renders, stylisation follows. The 104 keypoints come out of ANNY’s own forward kinematics, so the label is exact by construction and the rendered body is the body the keypoints describe. A skeletal disagreement between ANNY and a pose source violates no ground truth, because no ground truth is being compared: the source skeleton only has to supply plausible pose variety.
Everything below was measuring how closely ANNY could imitate the Kimodo gap corpus’s body. That is a question for retargeting a specific character, not for building a labelled corpus. sample_identities.py confirms the separation from the other side – identity and phenotype variation are their own pluggable axis with their own relations, not something a pose fit solves.



Bone lengths are pose-invariant, so they are what the fit targets; an earlier attempt compared ANNY’s rest pose against the corpus’s crouch frame and reported a mean near 552 mm – eight soda cans, which is a crouch and not a skeleton – and would have disproved a correct hypothesis. Residuals against the corpus’s 76 pose-invariant lengths, in millimetres, with a stacked penny at 1.52 mm:
